query: Which method can be used for oxidation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A machine-learning-driven framework that predicts optimal friction processing parameters can enhance oxidation resistance in refractory high-entropy alloys by producing a refined surface that promotes uniform, adherent protective oxide scale formation without modifying the bulk composition.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy exhibiting insufficient oxidation resistance and heterogeneous surface conditions under high-temperature exposure.
generation.intervention: Apply a data-driven machine learning model to existing high-throughput oxidation-test data in order to determine ideal friction processing or advanced surface treatment parameters that improve the formation of protective oxide scales.
generation.conditions: Isothermal oxidation at elevated temperatures (e.g., around 1000–1100°C) typical for high-temperature structural applications.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined, defect-reduced surface microstructure that facilitates the formation of a homogeneous, adherent oxide scale composed of protective compounds (e.g., CrTaO4, Al2O3).
generation.mechanism: Optimized friction processing removes surface defects and refines grain boundaries, which in turn enables a more uniform and coherent protective oxide scale. This scale acts as a diffusion barrier to oxygen, reducing further oxidation rates at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples receiving the machine-learning optimized friction processing treatment will demonstrate lower oxidation weight gain, improved oxide scale uniformity, and better adhesion compared to samples processed via conventional methods.
generation.baseline: Refractory high-entropy alloys processed with standard methods that do not employ data-driven optimization, showing higher and less controlled oxidation behavior.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies primarily under controlled high-temperature oxidation conditions and for alloy systems where surface treatment effects are the dominant factor over bulk compositional changes.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of oxidation resistance improvement is uncertain, as it depends on the quality and representativeness of the high-throughput data, the accuracy of the machine learning model, and the specific alloy composition used.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of refractory high-entropy alloy samples. One set is processed using the machine-learning predicted friction processing/surface treatment parameters while a control set is processed with conventional methods. Subject both sets to isothermal oxidation tests at 1100°C for 200 hours. Characterize and compare the oxidation weight gain, oxide scale morphology, and adhesion between the two sets.
measurements: Oxide scale microstructure and phase composition (via SEM/TEM and XRD)
Scale adhesion tests (e.g., scratch testing or peel tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples treated with the machine-learning optimized processing do not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in oxidation weight gain and improvement in oxide scale uniformity and adhesion when compared to the control group, the hypothesis is falsified.

Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ]. The concept of HEAs provides us an unprecedented degree of freedom in the design of advanced alloys with promising properties. For the rapid exploration of the vast compositional space and investigation of the composition and temperature effects on the microstructure, advanced HEA-design strategies and efficient tools are necessary. decision.trend: Over several iterations, researchers have explored various avenues to address insufficient oxidation resistance in generic high-entropy and refractory alloys. Early studies largely focused on chemical modifications (e.g., adding Cr, Al, Si) or incorporating ceramic reinforcements to form protective oxide scales (e.g., Al2O3, CrTaO4) at elevated temperatures. Later work investigated surface treatments such as fused-silicon coatings (Si–Cr–Fe) and grain-refining friction processes to enhance protective oxide formation and improve scale adhesion. Although these paths have shown some success in particular alloys and temperature ranges, no single strategy has emerged as a universal oxidation-resistance solution, especially for newly designed compositions and complex service conditions.
decision.unsolved: Despite progress in identifying beneficial elements (Cr, Al, Si) and adopting processing strategies (e.g., friction refining, surface coatings), predicting and optimizing oxidation resistance remains challenging. Difficulties persist in balancing mechanical performance with oxidation protection. A unifying, rapid, and predictive approach is needed to guide composition and microstructure selection without repeated trial-and-error experiments or exclusive reliance on adding more alloying elements.
decision.lever: Develop a machine-learning-driven design framework that links high-throughput oxidation-test data with composition and processing parameters, enabling rapid identification of protocols (e.g., friction processing conditions or advanced surface treatments) that optimize scale formation and substrate adhesion without altering the bulk composition.
decision.why: Past research has shown that while coating strategies, microstructural refinement, and compositional adjustments can help, a universal solution remains elusive. A data-driven model can capture and integrate existing large datasets on oxidation performance to quickly predict effective methods (like friction processing variables or surface modifications) for new or underexplored materials, accelerating the design of oxidation-resistant systems without resorting to repeated alloying additions.
